(Surat Fatir is Meccan, and it has forty-five verses.)

﴿All praise is due to Allah, Originator (Fatir) of the heavens and the earth﴾: the One who brings them into being (mubdi'uhuma) without any pattern to imitate or any model to follow. Fatir derives from fatr, which means splitting. It is said that fatr specifically means splitting lengthwise, as if He split non-existence (al-'adam) by bringing the two out of it. The idafa (construction) here is maḥḍa (pure, i.e. definite), because the participle carries the sense of the past tense; therefore Fatir is a descriptive adjective (na't) of the Glorious Name. Whoever considers the idafa non-pure (ghayr maḥḍa) makes it an apposition (badal) to the Name, though this is rare with a derived noun. ﴿Who made the angels﴾ (jā'ili al-malā'ika): the discussion about its idafa and whether it is a descriptive adjective or an apposition is the same as what came before it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿messengers﴾ (rusulan) is in the accusative governed by it (jā'il) according to the second aspect of the idafa, by general agreement. As for the first aspect, it is likewise so according to al-Kisa'i (d. 189 AH), whereas according to the Basrans it is governed by an implied verb that it indicates, because the active participle, when it carries the sense of the past tense, according to them does not govern except when it has the definite article (al-). Abu Sa'id al-Sirafi said: an active participle that is transitive to two objects governs the second, because by its idafa to the first, its idafa to the second became impossible, so its accusative reading was determined for it. Some scholars explained this by saying that by the idafa it resembles the definite article construction, so it governs as that does.

It was read as (jā'ilun) in the nominative, as a laudatory (madḥ) construction. It was also read: (alladhi fatara al-samawati wal-arda wa-ja'ala al-malā'ika), meaning: making them intermediaries (wasa'it) between Him, Exalted is He, and His prophets and the righteous among His servants, who convey to them His messages through revelation (wahy), inspiration (ilham), and true dreams; or between Him, Exalted is He, and His creation as well, in that they bring to them the traces of His power and His craftsmanship. This is on the assumption that the making is transformative (taṣyiriyyan). As for the assumption that it is originative (ibda'iyyan), then "rusulan" is in the accusative of circumstance (ḥāl). It was also read (rusalan) with a sukun on the sin.

﴿Possessors of wings﴾ (ulī ajniḥatin): a descriptive adjective of "rusulan". "Ulu" is a plural noun for "dhu" (possessor), just as "ula'ika" is a noun for "dha" (this), and their parallels among the declinable nouns are "al-makhad" and "al-khilfa".

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿two, three, and four﴾ (mathnā wa-thulātha wa-rubā') are descriptive adjectives of "ajniḥatin", meaning: possessors of multiple wings, varying in number according to the differing ranks they hold, with which they descend and ascend, or hasten. The meaning is that among the angels there are kinds, each one of which has two wings; kinds for whom each has three wings; and another kind for whom each has four wings.

It is narrated that a category of angels has six wings: with two of them they cover their bodies, with two others they fly in what they are commanded from His direction, exalted is He, and two of them are lowered over their faces out of shame before Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

And from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he saw Jibril (peace be upon him) on the night of the Ascension (mi'raj), and he had six hundred wings. And it is narrated that he asked him, peace be upon them both, to appear to him in his form; he said: "Indeed you will not be able to bear that." He said: "I love that you do it." So he (ﷺ) went out on a moonlit night, and Jibril, peace be upon them both, came to him in his form, and he (ﷺ) fainted, then regained consciousness, while Jibril was supporting him, with one of his hands on his chest and the other between his shoulders. He said: "Glory be to Allah! I did not think that any of creation was like this." Jibril, peace be upon him, said: "How then if you saw Israfil? He has twelve wings: one wing in the East and one wing in the West, and the Throne is upon his shoulder, and he shrinks at times out of the greatness of Allah, Exalted and Majestic, until he becomes like the wasa' (a tiny sparrow)," which is the small sparrow.

﴿He adds to creation what He wills﴾ (yazidu fi al-khalqi ma yasha'): a resumptive statement (istinaf) confirming what came before it regarding the variation in the states of the angels in the number of wings, and indicating that this is among the rulings of His will, Exalted is He, not due to a matter pertaining to their essences. It declares a general rule that He, Exalted is He, adds to whatever creation He wills whatever He wishes to add, in accordance with His will and the requirement of His wisdom, from matters that description cannot encompass.

As for what has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) about singling out some qualities for mention, such as the beautiful face, the beautiful voice, and the beautiful hair, it is an explanation of some of the known materials by way of example, not by way of restriction to them. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed Allah is over all things Competent﴾ (inna Allaha 'ala kulli shay'in qadir) is a justification, in the manner of affirmation, for the mentioned ruling, since the comprehensiveness of His power over all things necessitates His power to add whatever He wills, with clear necessity.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 35, verse 2:

﴿What Allah grants to mankind of mercy﴾ He expressed the sending of it by "opening" (fath), to indicate that it is the most precious of the treasures, over which competitors compete, and the most difficult to attain. Its indefiniteness (tankir) is for generality and vagueness, meaning: whatever Allah opens of the treasures of His mercy — any mercy whatsoever, of blessing, health, security, knowledge, wisdom, and other things that cannot be encompassed — ﴿none can withhold it﴾, that is, no one is able to withhold it; ﴿and whatever He withholds﴾, that is, whatever thing He withholds, ﴿none can release it after Him﴾, that is, no one is able to release it. The difference between the two pronouns is because the referent of the first is specified as mercy, while the referent of the second is unrestricted, encompassing it and other than it, whatever it may be; and in this there is an indication that His mercy precedes His wrath. ﴿After Him﴾, that is, after His withholding. ﴿And He is the Mighty﴾, the Overpowering over every matter He wills, among which are the opening and the withholding, ﴿the Wise﴾, who does everything He does according to what wisdom and benefit require. The sentence is a concluding remark (tadhyil) confirming what precedes it, and expressing that each of the opening and the withholding is in accordance with the wisdom on which the affair of creation revolves.

After He, glorified is He, had made clear that He is the originator of the dominion and the sovereignty, and the one who disposes of them by contraction and expansion, with no one having any part whatsoever in that, He addressed the people in general — or the people of Makkah in particular — regarding giving thanks for His blessings, saying:

"O people, remember God's favour upon you." That is, His bestowal upon you, if *ni'mah* is taken as a verbal noun (*masdar*), or "that which is upon you," if it is taken as a noun (*ism*). That is, observe it and preserve it by knowing its due, acknowledging it, and devoting worship and obedience exclusively to its Bestower. Since God's favours, despite the diversity of their kinds, are confined to the favour of bringing into existence and the favour of sustaining, He negated that there exists in being anything other than Him from which either of the two favours proceeds. He did so by way of a denying interrogative (*istifham inkari*), which calls for the impossibility of being answered with "yes." So He said: "Is there any creator other than God?" That is, does there exist a creator distinct from Him, Exalted is He? Here "creator" (*khaliq*) is the subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate (*khabar*) is omitted. The word "min" has been added to it to emphasise generality. "Other than God" (*ghayru Allah*) is an attributive modifier (*na't*) of it with respect to its position (*mahall*), just as it is a modifier of it in the reading with the genitive case (*jarr*) with respect to its wording (*lafz*). It has also been read in the accusative (*nasb*) as an exception (*istithna'*).

His saying, Exalted is He: "who provides for you from the heaven and the earth" (that is, with rain and plants) is a new sentence (*kalam mubtada'*) under all the possibilities of analysis, having no grammatical position (*mahall min al-i'rab*). It falls within the scope of the negation and denial. There is no justification for what has been said, that it is another attribute of "creator," in the nominative or genitive position, because its meaning is the negation of the existence of a creator described by both the attributes of being distinct and being a provider together, without addressing the negation of the existence of what is described merely by distinctness. Nor is there justification for what has been said, that it is the predicate of the subject, or that it is an explanation (*mufassir*) of a pronoun implied, which the phrase "from a creator" (*min khaliq*) takes as its agent in the subject role (*fa'iliyyah*), meaning: "Does a creator other than Him provide for you...?" For their meaning is the negation of the provision of a creator distinct from Him, Exalted is He, without addressing the negation of his existence altogether, although that is the decisive meaning. Do you not see that His saying, Exalted is He: "There is no god but He," is a resumed sentence (*isti'naf*) brought to confirm the negation that is primarily understood from it, and it operates as an answer to what the interrogative appears to imply in form? Since this sentence expresses the negation of existence, it is definitively necessary that this one too be so.

The particle "fa" in His saying, Exalted is He: "So how are you turned away?" is for ordering the denial of their deviation from monotheism to polytheism upon what precedes it, as if it were said: "And since it has become clear that He alone is the Deity, the Creator and the Provider, then in what manner are you turned away from monotheism to polytheism?"

His saying, Exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 35, verse 4:

﴿And if they deny you, then messengers before you were denied﴾ This is a shift of address (talwin al-khitab), turning the speech toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the midst of addressing the people. It is a hastening to console him (ﷺ) first by the generality of the affliction, and second by an allusion to the promise and the threat. That is: if they persist in denying you regarding what you have conveyed to them of the manifest truth, after you have established the proof against them and silenced them with the stone (alqamtahum al-hajar), then take example from those messengers in patient endurance (al-musabarah) over what afflicted them from the side of their peoples. The phrase mentioned has been placed in the position of that, by being content with mentioning the cause instead of mentioning the effect. The indefinite form "messengers" (rusul) is for magnification (al-tafkhim), which necessitates greater consolation and the orientation toward patient endurance. That is: messengers of great and momentous affair, and of great number.

﴿And to Allah are returned the affairs﴾ not to anything else, so that He will recompense each of you, you and them, according to the states you are in, of which among them are your patience and their denial. In restricting the return to Allah, the Exalted, together with the vagueness of the recompense, whether reward or punishment, there is an emphasis in promise and threat that is not hidden. It has been read as "tarji'" with a fatha on the ta', from the return (al-ruju'), and the first is more effective in inspiring awe (al-tahwil).

O mankind! ﴿O mankind!﴾ This returns to their address, and the repetition of the call serves to emphasise admonition and reminder. ﴿Indeed the promise of Allah﴾, referred to by the return of all affairs to Him, the Exalted, namely the resurrection (al-ba'th) and recompense (al-jaza'), ﴿is true﴾, established without doubt and without any failure to fulfil it. ﴿So let not the life of this world deceive you﴾, lest the enjoyment of its comforts distract you and its diversions with its adornments divert you from preparing for what concerns you on the day the appointed time arrives. The intended meaning is a prohibition against being deceived by it, even though the prohibition is outwardly directed at it, as in His, the Exalted, words: ﴿Let not my dissent lead you into sin﴾ and ﴿and let not the Deceiver deceive you concerning Allah﴾, and His pardon and generosity, the Exalted. ﴿The Deceiver﴾, that is, the one who is extreme in deception, namely Satan, who makes you wish for forgiveness while you persist in sins, saying: "Do whatever you wish, for Allah is Forgiving and forgives all sins." Although that is possible, to engage in sins with this expectation is like taking poison while relying on the body's ability to expel it. The repetition of the verb of prohibition is for emphasis, and because the two deceptions differ in manner. It is also recited as (al-ghurur) with a damma, as either a verbal noun (masdar), or the plural of ghar, like qu'ud as the plural of qa'id.

(p-144) ﴿Indeed, Satan is an enemy to you﴾: an ancient enmity that hardly ever ceases. The placing of "to you" (lakum) first serves to emphasize concern with it. ﴿So take him as an enemy﴾ by opposing him in your beliefs and your actions, and by being on guard against him in all the circumstances of your lives. His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He only invites his party that they may be among the companions of the Blaze﴾ is a confirmation of his enmity and a warning against obeying him, by alerting to the fact that his purpose in calling his followers to follow desire and to incline toward the comforts of this world is not to attain their worldly aims and benefits, as is the aim of loving friends in this world when some of them strive for the needs of others. Rather, it is to ruin them and cast them into everlasting punishment from where they do not perceive.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 35, verse 7:

﴿Those who disbelieve, for them﴾ — because of their disbelief, and their responding to the call of Satan, and their following his footsteps — ﴿is a severe punishment﴾, whose extent cannot be measured, and whose lasting duration cannot be reached. ﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds, for them﴾ — because of what has been mentioned of faith and righteous action, of which the enmity toward Satan is part — ﴿is forgiveness﴾, great, ﴿and a great reward﴾, the ultimate end for both of them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 35, verse 8:

﴿Is he, then, to whom the evil of his deeds has been made attractive, so that he sees it as good...?﴾ This is either a restatement of what preceded, namely the clear contrast between the final outcomes of the two groups, by explaining the contrast between their two conditions that lead to those two outcomes. The "fa" (fa, "then") is for denying that what follows it is a consequence of what precedes it. That is: after their conditions being as mentioned, is it [possible that] one to whom disbelief has been made attractive by Satan, so that he plunged into it, is like one who found it repugnant, avoided it, and chose faith and righteous deeds, so that their outcomes are not as mentioned? The part that was omitted was omitted because what came before indicates it.

And His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah leads astray...﴾ etc., is a confirmation of this and an establishing of the truth, by explaining that all of it is by His will, exalted is He. That is: indeed He, exalted is He, leads astray ﴿whom He wills﴾ to lead astray, because He approves and favours error and turns His choice toward it, so He casts him down to the lowest of the low. ﴿And guides whom He wills﴾ to guide, by turning His choice toward guidance, so He raises him to the highest of the high (ʿIlliyyin). Or it is a preparation for what follows of his ﷺ prohibition from grief and sorrow over them for their not becoming Muslims, by explaining that they are not deserving of that, but rather that he should turn away from them and not care for them at all. That is: after their condition being as mentioned, will you grieve over them? The part omitted is indicated by His saying: ﴿So do not let your soul go to waste in regret over them﴾, which is a clear indication. Or it is a preparation for turning him ﷺ away from the intense eagerness he had for their becoming Muslims, and from exerting great effort in calling them to it, by explaining the impossibility of their turning away from disbelief, since it is in its utmost beauty in their eyes. That is: after what has been mentioned of one to whom disbelief has been made attractive by Satan, so that he sees it as good and plunges into it, will he accept guidance so that you hope for his Islam and exhaust yourself in calling him to it? The part omitted is indicated by what passed of His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah leads astray whom He wills﴾ etc., showing that he is among those whom Allah, exalted is He, willed to lead astray. ﴿So who can guide one whom Allah has led astray? And for them there are no helpers.﴾ And it was read: (فَلا تُذْهِبْ نَفْسَكُ) [so do not cause your soul to go].

And His, exalted is He, saying ﴿hasarat﴾ [regrets] is either an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), meaning: "so do not let your soul perish for the regrets," and the plural is to indicate the multiplication of his ﷺ distress over their conditions, or over the abundance of their ugly deeds that call for regret and remorse. "ʿAlayhim" ('over them') is complementary to (tadhhab, "go"), as one says: "halaka ʿalayhi ḥubban" (he perished over him out of love) and "māta ʿalayhi ḥuznan" (he died over him from sorrow). Or it is an explanation of what is regretted over, and it is not permissible for it to be connected to (ḥasarat), because the verbal noun may not have its complement placed before it. Or it is a circumstantial clause (ḥal), as if all of them had become regrets.

And His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do﴾, meaning: of the ugly deeds, is a reason for what precedes it according to the three aspects, together with the threat it contains.

From Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl and the polytheists of Makkah.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 35, verse 9:

﴿Allah is He who sends the winds﴾ is a subject and predicate (mubtada' and khabar). It is also read as (al-rīḥa, "the wind," in the singular). The verb in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and they stir up clouds﴾, is in the present tense (ṣīghat al-muḍāri') to relate a past situation (ḥikāyat al-ḥāl al-māḍiyya), summoning that wondrous image which indicates the perfection of power and wisdom. It is also because the purpose is to explain its bringing about that property, and for this reason it is attributed to it (the wind). Or it is to indicate the continuation of the stirring up. ﴿Then We drive it to a dead land﴾, and it is also read with the lighter form (bi-l-takhfīf). ﴿And We give life thereby to the earth﴾, i.e., by the rain descending from it, which is indicated by the clouds, for there is a mutual implication (talāzum) between them in the mind, as in external reality; or by the clouds, for they are the cause of the cause. ﴿After its death﴾, i.e., its dryness. The two verbs are put in the form of the past tense to indicate certainty, and they are ascribed to the nun of majesty (nūn al-'aẓama), which announces their exclusivity to Him, Exalted is He, because of the greater craftsmanship in them, and to complete the resemblance between the giving of life to the earth and the resurrection, to which it is likened by His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Thus is the resurrection﴾, in the perfection of exclusivity to the Lordly power. The kāf is in the position of raising (ḥayyiz al-rafʿ) as a predicate (al-khabariyya), i.e., like that giving of life which you witness is the giving of life to the dead in the possibility of being decreed and the ease of its occurrence without any difference between them at all, except the alif in the first and not in the second. It has also been said: regarding the manner of the giving of life, God Exalted sends water from beneath the Throne, and from it the bodies of creation sprout.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 35, verse 10:

﴿Whoever desires honour⁠—﴾ they are the polytheists who would seek strength through worshipping idols, as in His saying, ﴿And they have taken gods besides Allah, that they might be for them a source of honour.﴾ And those who sought strength through them from among those who believed with their tongues [only], as in His saying, ﴿Those who take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers. Do they seek honour with them? Indeed, honour belongs entirely to Allah.﴾ The combination of (kāna, "was") and (yurīdu, "desires") serves to indicate the continuity and persistence of the desire. ﴿So to Allah belongs honour entirely﴾ i.e., to Him alone, not to other than Him, is the honour of this world and the honour of the Hereafter. That is, let them seek it from Him, not from other than Him. So mention of it is dispensed with by mentioning its evidence, signalling that the exclusivity of honour to Him, exalted is He, necessitates that the seeking of it be restricted to Him, exalted is He.

And His saying, exalted is He, ﴿To Him ascends the good word, and righteous deed raises it up﴾ is an explanation of what honour is sought by, namely tawhid (monotheism, the affirmation of God's oneness) and righteous deed. Their ascent to Him is a metaphor for His acceptance of them, or it refers to the ascent of the recording angels with their record. The placing of the prepositional phrase first (ilayhi, "to Him") is an expression of the complete importance attached to it, as in His saying, exalted is He, "And it is He who accepts repentance from His servants and takes charity." That is, to Him reaches the good word by which honour is sought, not only to the angels entrusted with the deeds of the servants. He honours its speaker and grants his request directly.

The pronoun in (yarfa'uhu, "raises it up") refers to the word (al-kalim); for the acceptance of deed depends on tawhid. This is supported by the reading with the accusative on (al-'amal, "the deed"), or (al-'amala, "the deed"), for it establishes faith and strengthens it, and lofty ranks are not attained except through it. It was also read (yusa''idu, "ascends") from (al-is'ad, "causing to ascend") in both voices (active and passive), and the one who causes it to ascend is Allah, glorified is He, or the one who speaks it, or the angel. It has been said: the good word encompasses remembrance, supplication, seeking forgiveness, and recitation of the Qur'an.

And it is narrated from him (ﷺ) that he said: "Glory be to Allah, all praise is due to Allah, there is no god but Allah, and Allah is greatest. When the servant says them, an angel carries them up to the heaven, and he greets with them the Face of the Most Merciful. But if he has not done a righteous deed, they are not accepted."

And it is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: No Muslim servant says five words: "Glory be to Allah, all praise is due to Allah, there is no god but Allah, Allah is greatest, and blessed is Allah," except that an angel takes them and places them beneath his wing, then ascends with them. He does not pass with them by a company of angels except that they seek forgiveness for the one who said them, until he greets with them the Face of the Lord of the worlds. Its confirmation is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿To Him ascends the good word⁠﴾... etc.

﴿And those who plot evil deeds⁠—﴾ is an explanation of the state of the evil word and the evil deed and their people, after the explanation of the state of the good word and the righteous deed. The accusative of (al-sayyi'at, "evil") is because it is an adjective of the omitted verbal noun, i.e., they plot evil plots. These are the plots of the Quraysh against the Prophet (ﷺ) in the Dar al-Nadwa (the assembly house of Quraysh), and their deliberation over one of three things: confining him (al-ithbat), killing him, or expelling him. ﴿For them⁠—﴾ because of their plots ﴿is a severe punishment⁠﴾ whose extent cannot be measured, and their plotting is not regarded at all in its presence. ﴿And the plot of those⁠—﴾ the demonstrative noun has been placed in the position of their pronoun, to signal the complete distinction of their state of evil and corruption above all other corrupters, and their notoriety for that, and the sense of distance in it serves to draw attention to the far-reaching nature of their affair in rebellion and the remoteness of their station in transgression. That is: and the plot of those corrupters who wished to plot against him (ﷺ) ﴿is one that will perish⁠﴾, i.e., it will itself be destroyed and ruined, not the ones against whom they plotted. Indeed, Allah, exalted is He, destroyed them after the destruction of their plots, when He expelled them from Mecca, killed them, and cast them into the well of Badr. Thus He gathered upon them their three plots, of which they had been content, against him (ﷺ), with only one of them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 35, verse 11:

﴿And Allah created you from dust﴾ is another proof of the soundness of the resurrection (al-ba'th) and the raising up (al-nushur). That is: He created you at the beginning from it, within the creation of Adam (peace be upon him), in a general (ijmali) manner, as has been established in its verification many times. ﴿Then from a drop of semen﴾, that is: then He created you from it in a detailed (tafsili) manner. ﴿Then He made you into pairs﴾, that is: kinds, or males and females. It is reported from Qatadah: He made some of you a spouse for others. ﴿No female bears or gives birth except with His knowledge﴾, except while it is accompanied by His knowledge and subject to His will. ﴿Nor is any aged person granted long life or has any of his life shortened﴾, that is: of anyone. He is called "aged" (mu'ammar) only with regard to his eventual end; that is: no one's life is extended except... [continuing the sense]: nor is any of anyone's life shortened, following the manner of their saying: Allah does not reward a servant nor punish him except with right; yet not in the sense that his life is shortened after having been increased, but in the sense that it is not made deficient from the beginning. It has also been said: the increase and decrease in the life of one person are with regard to different causes recorded in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh), such as writing in it: If so-and-so performs the pilgrimage (hajj), his life will be sixty years, and otherwise forty.

To this the Prophet (ﷺ) alluded when he said: "Charity and maintaining ties of kinship (al-silah) build up dwellings and increase lifespans." It has also been said: the intended "decrease" is what passes of his life and is diminished, for it is written in the record: his life is so-and-so years; then beneath that is written: a day has passed, two days have passed, and so on until it reaches its end. It was also read: (wa-la yanqusu), with the verb in the active voice, and (min 'umrihi) with the mim sukun (p-147).

﴿Except in a Book﴾. From Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him both) that it is the Preserved Tablet. It has also been said: the knowledge of Allah, Mighty and Majestic; and it has also been said: the record of each person. ﴿Indeed, that﴾, that is: what has been mentioned of creation and what follows it, together with its being a bewilderment to minds and understandings, ﴿is easy for Allah﴾, because He is free of need for causes; so likewise is the resurrection.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 35, verse 12:

﴿And the two seas are not alike: this one is sweet, fresh, pleasant for drinking, and that one is salty, bitter.﴾ It is a parable struck for the believer and the disbelievers. Al-Furat (the sweet, fresh water) is that which quenches thirst; al-sa'igh (pleasant) is that whose descent is easy because of its sweetness; and al-ujaj (bitter) is that which burns because of its saltiness. It has also been read as (sayyigh), like (sayyid), and as (sayg) with the lightened form, and (milh) like (katif).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and from each﴾, i.e., from each one of the two, ﴿you eat fresh flesh﴾, and ﴿you extract﴾, i.e., from the salty one specifically, ﴿ornaments which you wear﴾. This is either a digression in describing the two seas and the blessings and benefits in them, or a completion of the parable. The meaning is: just as the two, although they share some benefits, are not equal in respect of what is the primary purpose of water, because one of them has been mixed with what corrupts it and changes it from its perfect natural state, so the disbeliever is not equal to the believer, even though he shares with him some attributes such as courage, generosity and the like; because they differ in what is the greatest distinguishing feature, namely that one of them remains upon its original nature and attains its fitting perfection while the other does not. Or it is a preference of the bitter over the disbeliever, in that it shares with the sweet many benefits, whereas the disbeliever is entirely devoid of benefits, in the manner of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then your hearts became hardened after that, so they were like stones, or even harder. For indeed, among stones are those from which rivers gush forth, and indeed among them are those that split and water issues from them, and indeed among them are those that fall down out of fear of Allah﴾. What is meant by the ornament is pearls and coral. ﴿And you see the ships therein﴾, i.e., in each of them. The singular form of the address, despite the plural in what precedes and follows, is because the address is to every person who is able to see, not only to those who benefit from the two seas. ﴿Ploughing﴾, i.e., cutting through the water by their passage, advancing and retreating with one wind. ﴿That you may seek of His bounty﴾, i.e., of Allah's bounty, by travelling in them. The "lam" is connected to (ploughing); it has also been permitted that it be connected to what the mentioned verbs indicate, i.e., He did that so that you might seek of His bounty. ﴿And that you may be grateful﴾, i.e., and that you might give thanks for that. The particle of hope (la'alla) is to signal that this is pleasing to Allah, exalted is He.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 35, verse 13:

﴿He causes the night to enter into the day﴾, by increasing one of them and decreasing the other, by adding some parts of each of them to the other. ﴿And He has subjected the sun and the moon﴾ is conjoined to (yuliju, "He causes to enter"), and the difference between them in form (ṣīghah, grammatical form) is because the entering of one of the two alternating phases into the other is renewed moment after moment. As for the subjugation of the two luminaries, it is a matter with no multiplicity in it; what is multiple and renewed are its effects.

This is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Each runs﴾, i.e., according to its own particular motion and its compelled motion on the multiple daily orbits, according to the multiplicity of the days of the year, running continuously, ﴿for a term specified﴾ (p-148) which Allah, exalted is He, has determined for their running, and it is the Day of Resurrection, as has been narrated from al-Hasan, may Allah have mercy on him.

It has also been said: their running is an expression for their two particular motions in their two orbits, and the specified term is the endpoint of their two cycles. The duration of the running is a year for the sun and a month for the moon, and its detail has already passed in Surat Luqman. ﴿That is﴾ is a reference to the agent of the aforementioned acts, and the sense of distance in it is to signal the utmost of greatness. It is the subject (mubtada'), and what follows it are successive predicates (akhbar mutaradifah), i.e., that is the One of great rank who originated these wondrous works. ﴿Allah is your Lord; His is the dominion﴾. In it is a clear indication that His originating those wonders, exalted is He, necessitates the establishment of those predicates for Him, which is not hidden. It is also permissible that the last clause be an independent statement, in contrast to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those you call upon besides Him do not possess [even] a fine membrane of a date pit﴾, to indicate His sole being the One deserving divinity and lordship. It has been read as (yad'ūna) with the letter ya' (third person). Al-qiṭmīr (qitmir, a fine membrane of a date pit) is the thin covering of the date stone, and it is a proverb for scantiness and insignificance.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 35, verse 14:**

﴿If you call upon them, they will not hear your call﴾ is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*) that confirms the content of what precedes it and reveals the clear state of what you call upon: that it is inanimate, and that hearing is not among its attributes. ﴿And even if they were to hear﴾, supposing and assuming it, ﴿they would not respond to you﴾, because they are utterly incapable of acts. This is not because of what some have said, that they will disown you and disown what you ascribe to them, for that is not conceivable from them in this world. ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will disavow your association﴾, meaning they will deny that you associated them with Him and worshipped them, by their saying: ﴿You never used to worship us﴾. ﴿And none can inform you like one who is all-aware﴾, meaning no informant can tell you the matter as one who is all-aware has informed you of it, and that is the Truth, glorified is He, for He is the one who knows the reality of affairs, to the exclusion of all other informants. The purpose is to affirm what He has reported about the condition of their gods and to negate what they claim for them of divinity.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 35, verse 15:

﴿O mankind, you are the poor (fuqara') before Allah﴾ in your selves, and in whatever matter of importance occurs to you, or calamity that befalls you. The definite form "the poor" (al-fuqara') is used for emphasis (mubalaghah) regarding their poverty, as if, because of the abundance of their need and the severity of their dependence, they alone are "the poor," and the dependence of all other creatures, compared with their poverty, is like non-existence. For this reason, the Exalted said: ﴿And man was created weak﴾, and ﴿Allah is the Self-Sufficient (al-Ghani), the Praiseworthy (al-Hamid)﴾, that is: the One who is absolutely free of need (al-mustaghni 'ala al-iṭlaq), the Bestower of blessings upon all existing things, the One deserving of praise (al-mustawjib li-l-hamd).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 35, verse 16:

﴿If He wills, He will take you away and bring a new creation.﴾ They would not be in your attribute; rather, they would be steadfast in obedience, or [He would bring] another world different from what you know.
"And that is not difficult for Allah" — that is, what was mentioned of removing them and bringing others in their place is not hard for Allah, nor is it difficult or burdensome for Him.

﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾, that is, no sinful soul shall bear the sin of another soul. Rather, each of them bears only its own burden. As for His saying, ﴿And they shall surely bear their own burdens and burdens along with their burdens﴾, concerning the bearing by those who mislead others of burdens other than their own, it is the bearing of the burdens of their misguiding along with the burdens of their own error. Both are their own burdens, and nothing of the burdens of others is among them. ﴿And if a laden one calls [another] to its load﴾, that is, a soul weighed down by burdens calls someone ﴿to its load﴾ so that he will bear some of its burdens, ﴿nothing of it will be borne﴾, meaning it will not be answered by bearing any part of it. ﴿Even if he were one of near kinship﴾, that is, the one called, who is understood from the calling, is ﴿one of near kinship to the caller﴾. It is also read as "dhu qurba." This is a negation of bearing by choice, whereas the first clause negates it by compulsion. ﴿You only warn﴾ is a resumptive clause brought to explain who will be admonished by what has been mentioned. That is, you warn only with these warnings, ﴿those who fear their Lord unseen﴾. That is, they fear Him, the Exalted, while absent from His punishment, or absent from people in their solitude, or they fear His punishment while it is unseen by them. ﴿And establish the prayer﴾, that is, they observe it as it should be observed and make it a standing signpost and a raised banner. That is, your warning and admonition benefit only these people of your nation, and not others among the rebellious and obstinate. ﴿And whoever purifies himself﴾, that is, is cleansed of the filth of sins and disobedience by being affected by these warnings, ﴿then he purifies himself for his own self﴾, because its benefit is confined to himself, just as whoever is defiled by it is defiled only to his own harm. It is also read as "man izzakka fa-innama yuzakka." This is an interjected clause affirming their fear of Allah and their establishment of the prayer, since it is among the chief foundations of purification. ﴿And to Allah is the destination﴾, not to anyone else, either independently or jointly, so He will reward them for their purification with the best of rewards.
[Qur'an 35:19] "And the blind and the seeing are not alike." That is: the disbeliever and the believer.

And not the darknesses and not the light. That is: neither falsehood nor truth. The plural "darknesses" is used along with the singular "light" because the kinds of falsehood are many, whereas truth is one.

﴿Nor the shade and the heat﴾. That is: nor reward and punishment. The placing of "lā" before the two opposites serves to remind of the negation of equality, and its insertion between them is for emphasis. "Al-Ḥarūr" is on the pattern of faʿūl, from ḥarr (heat), and has become specifically applied to the scorching wind (al-samūm). It is said: al-samūm is what blows by day, and al-ḥarūr is what blows by night.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 35, verse 22:

﴿And the living are not equal to the dead.﴾ This is another parable for the believers and the disbelievers (p-150), more eloquent than the first. For this reason the verb was repeated, and the plural form was chosen for both parties, to affirm the contrast between the individuals of the two groups. It has also been said: it is a parable for the scholars and the ignorant. ﴿Indeed, Allah makes hear whom He wills﴾, that is, He causes him to hear and grants him success in understanding His verses and in taking admonition from His admonitions. ﴿But you cannot make hear those who are in the graves.﴾ This is a supporting indication (tarshih) for the parable of those who persist in disbelief being like the dead, and an emphatic statement (ishba') regarding the despair of the Prophet (ﷺ) over their faith.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 35, verse 23:

﴿You are only a warner.﴾ Your duty is only to warn. As for making them hear (al-Isma') absolutely, that is not among your duties, and you have no means to it with regard to those whose hearts have been sealed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 35, verse 24:

﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth﴾ That is: as those who are right (muhiqqin), or you (sent) as one who is right, or a sending accompanied by the truth. It is also permissible for it to be connected to His saying: ﴿as a bearer of good tidings and a warner﴾, that is: a bearer of good tidings of the true promise, and a warner of the true threat.

﴿And there is not a nation﴾ That is: there is no nation among the nations that passed away in past times ﴿but a warner had passed among them﴾ That is: had gone by, ﴿from a prophet or a scholar who warns them. The mention of only the warner suffices, since it is known that warning is the companion of good tidings, especially as the two have been mentioned together just before; and because warning is the more fitting to the context.

And if they deny you, [O Muhammad], then those before them also denied, meaning: persist in your denial, so do not concern yourself with them or with their denial. ﴿Then those before them also denied﴾ from the arrogant nations, ﴿their messengers came to them with the clear proofs﴾, that is, the manifest miracles indicating their prophethood, ﴿and with the scriptures﴾ such as the scrolls of Ibrahim (Ibrahim, Abraham), ﴿and with the illuminating Book﴾ such as the Torah (al-Tawrah), the Gospel (al-Injil), and the Psalms (al-Zabur), on the intention of detailing rather than combining. It is also permissible that both refer to one thing, and the conjunction (waw) is for the difference of the two designations.

Verse 26: ﴿Then I seized those who disbelieved﴾. The relative pronoun is placed in the position of their pronoun, to censure them by what is in the clause that follows it, and to indicate the cause of the seizing. ﴿So how was My rejection?﴾ That is: My disapproval by way of punishment. In this there is further intensification and awe-inspiring force regarding it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 35, verse 27:

﴿Have you not seen﴾ is a resumptive statement (istintaf) given to confirm what precedes it concerning the variation in the conditions of people, by showing that variation and differentiation is a constant matter in all created things, whether plants, inanimate objects, or animals. The seeing (ru'ya) here is of the heart (qalbiyya), meaning: Do you not know ﴿that Allah sent down water from the sky, and We brought forth by it﴾ by means of that water. The shift (iltifat) to the first person plural is to show full attention to the act, because of the wondrous craftsmanship in it that indicates perfect power and wisdom. ﴿fruits of diverse colors﴾ meaning their kinds (ajnas) or their varieties (asnaf), on the basis that each of them has various different varieties; or their forms (hay'at) and shapes (ashkal); or their colors (alwan), such as yellow, green, red and others. The last is the most fitting in light of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And of the mountains are streaks﴾ meaning possessing streaks (judad), that is, lines (khutat) and paths (taraq). It is said: "jiddat al-himar" for the black line on the back of the donkey (p-151).

It was also read as (judud), with a damma, the plural of (jadida), meaning freshness (jiddah); and (jadad), with two fathas, which is the clear path. ﴿white and red, diverse in their colors﴾ in intensity and weakness, ﴿and jet-black﴾ is coordinated (atf) with (white) or with (streaks). It is as if it were said: And of the mountains are striped ones possessing streaks, and among them are those of one color, jet-black (gharabib). It is an emphatic (ta'kid) for an implied term that is explained by what follows it, for gharib is an emphasis for black, like faqi' for yellow and qani for red. It is required of emphasis that it follow what it emphasizes. Its parallel in description is the verse of al-Nabigha:

"And the faithful one, the birds of the sanctuary stroking it"

Such emphasis, in a case like this, adds further emphasis to what contains repetition in terms of implicit and explicit mention.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 35, verse 28:

﴿And among mankind and the creatures that move and the cattle, there are those whose colours are various.﴾ That is: among them there are some whose colours are various, or some of them have various colours, as has passed in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among mankind is he who says, "We believe in Allah"﴾. The two clauses are introduced as nominal sentences, although they share with the verbal clause before them in the use of their content as evidence for the differences among people in inner states, because the variation of the mountains, people, creatures and cattle in the colours mentioned is a continuous matter, so it is expressed by what indicates continuity.

As for the bringing forth of the diverse fruits, since it is a matter that has come into being, it is expressed by what indicates occurrence. Then, since there is a kind of obscurity in it, He attached seeing to it by way of the interrogative of affirmation (istifham taqriri), which indicates the urging toward it and the encouragement to it, unlike the states of the mountains, people and others, for they are an observed matter that does not need reflection. Therefore they were stripped of being attached to seeing. So reflect.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus﴾ is a noun of comparison (masdar tashbihi) for His saying, exalted is He: "mukhtalif" (varying), that is, an attribute of its emphatic verbal noun. Its estimate is: "it varies with a variation that is of this kind", that is, like the variation of the fruits and the mountains. It was read "alwanan" and it was read "wal-dawab" with lightening (of the hamza or doubling), as an exaggeration in fleeing from the meeting of two quiescent letters (iltiqa' al-sakinayn).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Only those among His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾ is a completion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You can only warn those who fear their Lord unseen﴾, by specifying who among mankind fears Him, exalted and majestic is He, after explaining the variation of their classes and the difference of their ranks. As for the immaterial attributes, it is by way of representation (tamthil); as for the physical attributes, it is by way of explicit statement (tasrih), giving each of the two its due appropriate explanation. That is: only those who know Him, exalted and majestic is He, and what befits Him of His glorious attributes and His beautiful acts, fear Him unseen. This is because the basis of fear is knowledge of the one feared and knowing His affairs; so whoever knows Him, exalted is He, more is he fearful of Him, exalted and majestic is He, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: ﴿I am the most fearful of you of Allah and the most mindful of Him﴾. For this reason He followed it with mention of His acts that indicate the perfection of His power. And since the disbelievers are far from this knowledge, warning them in totality was impossible. The fronting of the object is because the intended purpose is to restrict the agency (hasr al-fa'iliyyah); had it been delayed, the matter would have been reversed.

It was read with the majestic Name in the nominative and "al-'ulama'" in the accusative, on the basis that fear is used metaphorically for veneration, for the one who is venerated is awe-inspiring. ﴿Indeed Allah is Mighty, Forgiving﴾ is a reason for the obligation of fear, because it indicates that He punishes the one who persists in his transgression, and forgives the one who repents of his disobedience.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 35, verse 29:

﴿Indeed, those who recite the Book of Allah﴾ meaning: they persist in reciting it, or in following what is in it, until this became a mark of them and a title for them. By "the Book of Allah, exalted is He," the Qur'an is meant. It has been said that it refers to the genus of the books of Allah, so that it would be praise of the believers among the peoples after the account of the condition of the deniers among them. But this is not the case, for the present tense (sigha al-mudari') indicates the continuing legislation of its recitation and acting upon what is in it, and their being followed by what will come of the full payment of rewards and the increase of bounty. To interpret it as narrating a past state, which is a manifest forcing of the meaning, is something with no way to it. How could it be otherwise! The purpose is the encouragement toward the religion of Islam and acting by the Qur'an, which abrogates what came before it of the books. So addressing the explanation of its reality before its abrogation, and elaborating on mentioning the great benefits that follow from it, is what produces desire for its recitation and turning toward acting by it. Restricting the recitation to what has not been abrogated from it is clearly invalid, since what remains legislated is nothing but its ruling, yet not insofar as it is its ruling but insofar as it is the ruling of the Qur'an. As for its recitation, it is entirely outside the legislated status and the entailment of reward, so reflect.

﴿and establish the prayer and spend from what We have provided them, secretly and openly﴾ in whatever manner it happens, without intending either of them specifically. It has been said that "secretly" refers to the recommended (masnunah) acts and "openly" to the obligatory (mafrudah) ones. ﴿They hope for a commerce﴾ meaning obtaining the reward of obedience, and this is the predicate of "inna" (indeed).

And the words of the Exalted: ﴿that will never perish﴾ meaning: it will never be unprofitable and will never be ruined by loss at all. It is an attribute of (commerce), brought in to indicate that it is not like the other trades which revolve between profit and loss, because it is a purchase of what remains in exchange for what passes away. And the report of their hope from the Most Generous of the generous is a definitive promise of the attainment of what they hope for.

And the words of the Exalted:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 35, verse 30:

﴿That He may pay them their rewards in full⦆ is connected to "لَنْ تَبُورَ" (lan tabur, "will never perish"), in the sense that decline is negated from it, and it is accepted with Allah the Exalted so that He may pay them the rewards of their deeds. ﴿And increase them of His bounty﴾ beyond that, from the treasuries of His mercy, what He wills. It was also said: it is connected to a hidden element indicated by what was enumerated of their pleasing deeds, meaning: they did that "li-yuwaffiyahum" (so that He may pay them) ... etc. It was also said: it is connected to "yarjuna" (they hope), on the basis that the lam is of consequence (lam al-'aqibah, the lam of outcome). ﴿Indeed He is Forgiving, Most Appreciative﴾ is a justification for what precedes it of paying in full and increasing, meaning: Forgiving of their lapses, Appreciative of their acts of obedience, i.e., rewarding them for them. It was also said: it is the predicate of "inna alladhina" (indeed those who), and "yarjuna" is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the waw of "anfaqu" (they spent).

"And that which We have revealed to you of the Book" — this is the Qur'an. The "min" (from) here is either for clarification (tabyin), or it denotes the genus (jins) with "min" being partitive (tab'id). It has been said that "the Book" refers to the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh), with "min" indicating origin (ibtida').

﴿It is the truth, confirming what is before it⦆ — that is, I make it (the Qur'an) the truth, confirming what preceded it of the heavenly Books. The phrase "confirming" is an emphatic circumstantial clause (hal mu'akkida), because its being the truth necessarily entails its agreement with them in the creeds and the fundamentals of the legal rulings. ﴿Indeed Allah is, concerning His servants, All-Aware, All-Seeing﴾ — He encompasses the inner states and outward conditions of their affairs. So had there been in your circumstances anything contrary to prophethood, He would not have revealed to you such a truth, miraculous and a criterion over all the other Books. The placing of "Aware" (khabir) first serves to alert to the fact that the principal concern is spiritual matters.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 35, verse 32:

﴿Then We caused the Book to be inherited﴾ That is: We decreed its being bequeathed to you (O Muhammad), or We shall bequeath it. The expression in the past tense is for its certainty and assured realization. It was also said: We caused it to be inherited from the earlier nations, that is, We delayed it from them and gave it ﴿to those whom We have chosen from among Our servants﴾. They are the scholars of this community from among the Companions and those who came after them who follow their way; or the whole community, for Allah the Exalted chose them over all other nations and made them ﴿a middle nation, that you may be witnesses over the people﴾, and singled them out with the honor of belonging to the best of His messengers, upon them be prayers and peace. Inheriting the Book does not necessarily entail observing it with its due observance, as indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then there succeeded them a succession who inherited the Book﴾ ... to the end of the verse. ﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself﴾ by falling short in acting upon it, and this is the one deferred to the command of Allah. ﴿And among them is one who is moderate﴾, acting upon it for the most part, though not free from mixing in some wrongdoing. ﴿And among them is one who outstrips in good deeds by Allah's permission﴾. It was said: they are the foremost, the first of the Emigrants and the Helpers. It was also said: they are those who persist in upholding its obligations in knowledge, action and teaching. In His saying "by Allah's permission", that is, by His facilitation and enabling, there is an alert to the difficulty of attaining this rank and the hardship of its path. It was also said: the one who wrongs himself is the ignorant, the moderate is the learner, and the outstripper is the scholar. It was also said: the one who wrongs himself is the sinner, the moderate is one who mixed good with evil, and the outstripper is one whose good deeds outweigh his evil deeds to the extent that his evil deeds become expiating. This is the meaning of the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "As for those who outstripped, they will enter Paradise and be provided therein without reckoning. As for the moderate, they will be reckoned with an easy reckoning. As for those who wronged themselves, they will be held back for a long time at the gathering, then Allah the Exalted will receive them with His mercy."

It has been narrated that 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), while on the pulpit, said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Our foremost is foremost, our moderate is saved, and our wrongdoer is forgiven."

﴿That﴾ refers to outstripping in good deeds, and the sense of distance in it, despite the nearness of the time of what is indicated, is to convey the loftiness of its rank and the remoteness of its station in honor ﴿it is the great bounty﴾ from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, which is not attained except by His enabling, Exalted is He.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 35, verse 33:

﴿Gardens of Eden﴾ is either a substitute (badal) for ﴿the great bounty﴾, by treating the cause as if it were the effect (tanzil al-sabab manzilat al-musabbab), or it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is ﴿they will enter them﴾. On the first reading it is a resumptive (mustaʼnaf) clause. The pronoun is in the plural because the intended meaning of "the foremost" (al-sabiqun) is the category as a whole. The mention of the condition and final destiny of the foremost alone, with silence about the other two groups, although this does not indicate that they are barred from entering Paradise absolutely, nonetheless contains a warning to them against negligence and an incitement to strive to attain the rank of the foremost.

It is also read as ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾ and ﴿Garden of Eden﴾ in the accusative (nasb), governed by a verb implied by the apparent word that follows. It is also read as ﴿they will be made to enter it﴾ in the passive voice (bina' lil-maf'ul). ﴿They will be adorned therein﴾ is a second predicate, or a presumed circumstantial clause (hal muqaddarah). It is also read as ﴿they will adorn﴾ from "haliyat al-mar'ah" (the woman adorned herself), so the form is ḥāliyah. ﴿With bracelets﴾: it is the plural of asāwir, which is the plural of siwār. ﴿Of gold﴾: the first "min" (min) is partitive (tab'idiyyah), and the second is explicative (bayaniyyah), meaning: they will be adorned with some bracelets of gold, as if it were the most excellent of all its kinds. ﴿And pearls﴾ is in the accusative, conjoined to the place (mahall) of "min asawir". It is also read in the genitive, conjoined to "gold", meaning: of gold set with pearls, or of gold in the purity of pearls. ﴿And their clothing therein is silk﴾: the change of style has already been discussed in surah al-Hajj.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 35, verse 34:

﴿And they will say﴾ i.e., they say. The past tense form is used to indicate certainty. ﴿"All praise is due to Allah, who has removed from us the grief"﴾, meaning that which troubled them, namely the fear of an evil end.

And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: (it is) the grief of calamities and afflictions; and from him: the grief of death.

And from al-Dahhak: the grief is the whisperings of Iblis (Satan).

It has been said: the concern of livelihood.

It has been said: the grief (p-154) of the loss of blessings.

The apparent meaning is that it is the generic noun encompassing all the griefs of the religion and of the world. It was also read as (al-Huzn).

And from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "There is no desolation upon the people of (There is no god but Allah) in their graves, nor in their gathering place, nor in their journey. And it is as if I see the people of (There is no god but Allah) coming out of their graves, shaking the dust from their faces, and saying: 'All praise is due to Allah, who has removed from us the grief.'"

﴿Indeed, our Lord is All-Forgiving﴾, i.e., to the sinners, ﴿Most Appreciative﴾, i.e., to the obedient.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 35, verse 35:

﴿Who has settled us in the abode of permanence﴾, that is, the abode of settlement from which there is never any removal, ﴿by His bounty﴾, by His favor and His grace, without anything on our part obligating Him to it. ﴿No fatigue touches us therein﴾, that is, toil, ﴿nor does weariness touch us therein﴾, that is, exhaustion. The difference between them is that _naṣab_ (fatigue) is the very hardship and burden, while _lughūb_ (weariness) is the lassitude that results from it. The explicit negation of the second, together with the fact that negating the first entails negating it, and the repetition of the negated verb (touches), are for the sake of emphasis in clarifying the absence of each of them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 35, verse 36:

﴿And those who disbelieve, for them is the fire of Hell; it shall not be decreed upon them﴾ — i.e., it shall not be judged against them that they die a second death, ﴿so that they should die﴾ and be at rest. Its being in the subjunctive is by the implied (an) [the particle "an", "that"]. It was also read: (fa-yamūtūna, "and they die"), in coordination with (yuqḍā, "it is decreed"), like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nor will they be given leave to make excuse﴾, and ﴿nor will its punishment be lightened for them﴾. Rather, whenever it subsides, its blaze is increased. ﴿Thus﴾, i.e., like that dreadful recompense, ﴿We recompense every ingrate﴾, one who exaggerates in disbelief (kufr) or ingratitude (kufrān), not a lighter and lesser recompense than that. It was also read: (yujzā, "is recompensed"), with the passive form, attributing it to the whole, and it was read: (yujāzā, "is requited").

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 35, verse 37:

﴿And they will cry out therein﴾ (yastaghithun, "they will seek relief"). Al-istiraakh (al-istirkh) is an iftiʿal form derived from al-suraakh (shouting), used for seeking help, because the one seeking help strains his voice. ﴿Our Lord, bring us out, that we may do righteous deeds, other than what we used to do﴾. The verb of saying is elided (bi-idmar al-qawl, "with the verb of saying omitted"). Restricting the righteous deed by the mentioned description (ghayr alladhi kunna naʿmal) expresses regret over what they did of other than righteous deeds, acknowledgment of it, and an indication that their being brought out is for the purpose of rectifying it, and that they used to think it was righteous, but now it has become clear that the opposite is the case.

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿Did We not give you a life long enough that whoever would be mindful could be mindful therein?﴾ is a reply from Him, the Exalted, and a rebuke to them. The hamza (alif al-istifham) is for denial and negation, and the waw is for conjunction upon an implied element required by the context. The word "ma" is an indefinite qualifying noun (nakira mawsufa), meaning: Did We not give you respite, or: Did We not delay you and not grant you a lifespan ('umran) in which ﴿whoever would be mindful could be mindful therein﴾, i.e., in which the one who takes heed is able to be mindful and reflect. It has been said that this is forty years, and it is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it is sixty years; this is also reported from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, and it is the lifespan by which Allah has left no excuse for the son of Adam.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah has left no excuse for a man whose term He delayed until he reached sixty years."

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿And the warner came to you﴾ is a conjunction upon the interrogative sentence, because it carries the meaning of "We have indeed given you a lifespan." Likewise in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ and ﴿And We laid down﴾ ... etc., because it carries the meaning of "We have indeed expanded..." etc. By "the warner" is meant the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) or what came with him of the Qur'an. It has been said: reason (al-ʿaql), and it has been said: gray hair (al-shayb), and it has been said: the death of relatives. Restricting the mention to the warner is because that is what the context requires. The "fa" in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So taste﴾ indicates the sequencing of the command to taste upon what precedes it of granting a lifespan and the coming of the warner. And in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So the wrongdoers will have no helper﴾ it is for causation (lil-taʿlil).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 35, verse 38:

﴿Indeed, Allah is the Knower of the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾ with the genitive construction (bi-l-idafa). It is also read with tanwin and with the accusative "ghayb" as its object (al-maf'uliyya), meaning: nothing hidden in them escapes Him, so their states are not concealed from Him. ﴿Indeed, He is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾. It has been said that this is a reason (ta'lil) for what precedes it, because when He knows the hidden thoughts within the breasts, which are the most concealed of things, He is all the more knowing of other things.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 35, verse 39:

﴿He is the One who has made you successors (khala'if) upon the earth.﴾ One who is made a successor is called khalifah, and the first (khala'if) is its plural, while the second (khulafa') is also its plural. The meaning is that He, exalted is He, has made you His successors (khulafa') in His earth, has cast into your hands the keys of disposal over it, has given you authority over what is in it, and has permitted you its benefits. Or [the meaning is that] He has made you successors of the nations that came before you, and has bequeathed to you what was in their hands of the goods of this world, so that you may give thanks to Him through monotheism and obedience. ﴿So whoever disbelieves﴾ among you, despite this lofty blessing, and spurns it, ﴿upon him is his disbelief﴾, i.e., the burden of his disbelief, which does not pass beyond him to others.

His exalted saying: ﴿And the disbelief of the disbelievers does not increase them, in the sight of their Lord, except in abhorrence; and the disbelief of the disbelievers does not increase them except in loss.﴾ This is an explanation of the burden and the harm of disbelief, namely God's abhorrence of them, i.e., His intense hatred, beyond which there is no disgrace or humiliation, and the loss of the Hereafter, beyond which there is no worse loss. The repetition is for the increase of emphasis and to draw attention to the fact that disbelief necessarily entails each of the two terrible and ugly outcomes independently and directly.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 35, verse 40:

﴿Say﴾ as a rebuke to them: ﴿Tell me about your associates whom you invoke besides Allah﴾, i.e., your gods. The attribution to them (your associates) is because they made them associates of Allah, the Exalted, without there being any basis for it whatsoever. It has been said that they made them associates to themselves in what they possess, but the flow and context of the noble composition reject this. ﴿Show me what they created of the earth﴾ is a badal al-ishtimal (inclusive apposition) from ﴿Tell me﴾, as if it were said: Inform me about your associates; show me what part of the earth they created. ﴿Or do they have a share in the heavens?﴾ i.e., do they have a partnership with Allah, glorified is He, in the creation of the heavens, so that they would thereby deserve a share in divinity in essence? ﴿Or have We given them a Book﴾ speaking that We have taken them as associates? ﴿So they are upon a clear proof from it﴾, i.e., an evident argument from that Book that they have a share by appointment. It is also permissible that the pronoun in (We have given them) refers to the polytheists, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or have We sent down to them any authority?﴾ ... etc. It is also read as (upon clear proofs), and this implies that polytheism is a grave matter, for its establishment requires the convergence of proofs. ﴿Rather, the wrongdoers promise one another nothing but delusion﴾. When he negated the kinds of proofs regarding this, he turned away from it by mentioning what moved them to it, namely the deception of predecessors to successors, and the misguidance of leaders for followers, by claiming that they are intercessors with Allah who intercede for them to draw near to Him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 35, verse 41:

(p-156) ﴿Indeed, Allah holds back the heavens and the earth lest they cease [to exist]﴾. This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) brought to explain the utmost ugliness of association (shirk) and that it is [utterly unfitting] for Him. That is: He holds them [in place] out of aversion to their ceasing, or He prevents them from ceasing, since holding back (al-imsak) is a form of preventing. ﴿And if they were to cease, none could hold them back after Him﴾. That is: none could hold them back [if He did not hold them]. "After Him" means after His holding them, the Exalted, or after their ceasing. The clause fills the place of both answers (saddat masadda al-jawabayn). The first "min" (from/any) is extra (za'idah) for emphasizing generality, and the second "min" denotes the starting point (li-l-ibtida'). ﴿Indeed He is ever Forbearing, Forgiving﴾: He does not hasten to the punishment that their transgressions would merit, in that He holds them back, although they were deserving of being crushed to pieces, as the Exalted said: ﴿The heavens are almost rent asunder from above them, and the earth is split open﴾. It is also read: (وَلَوْ زالَتا) [wa-law zalatā, "and even if they were to cease"].

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 35, verse 42:

﴿And they swore by God with their most solemn oaths that if a warner came to them, they would be better guided than any one of the (other) nations﴾. It reached Quraysh, before the mission of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), that the People of the Book had denied their messengers. So they said: "May God curse the Jews and the Christians! Messengers came to them and they denied them. By God, if a messenger comes to us, we will surely be better guided than any one of the nations: the Jews, the Christians, and others, or than the community that is called 'one of the nations' (ihda al-umam), preferring it over the others in guidance and uprightness." ﴿But when a warner came to them﴾ - and what a warner! The most honourable of the messengers, upon them be blessings and peace - ﴿it only increased them in aversion﴾, that is, the warner or his coming, ﴿[in] aversion﴾, distancing themselves from the truth.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 35, verse 43:**

﴿Arrogance in the land﴾ is either a substitute (badal) for (nufuran, "aversion"), or an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu). ﴿And the evil plotting﴾: its original form is "wa-in makaru al-sayyi'," meaning "al-makr al-sayyi'" (the evil plotting), then "wa-makra al-sayyi'," then "wa-makra al-sayyi'." It was also read with the hamza silent in connected speech, though this is probably an *ikhtilas* (a rapid, partial vocalization) that was taken to be silence or a slight pause. It was also read as "makran sayyi'an" (evil plotting, in the accusative). ﴿And the evil plotting does not encompass anyone except its own people. So are they waiting﴾, that is: what are they awaiting ﴿except the way (sunnat) of the former peoples﴾, that is, the way of God regarding them, by punishing their deniers. ﴿So you will not find any change in the way of God﴾, by which He would place something other than punishment in the place of punishment. ﴿And you will not find any alteration in the way of God﴾, by which He would transfer it from the deniers to others.

The "fa'" (so) indicates the cause of what the ruling implies, namely their awaiting the punishment's coming. The negation of finding any substitution (tabdil) and alteration (tahwil) is an expression of the negation of their existence by way of demonstrative proof. Singling out each of the two with a separate negation serves to emphasize the absence of both.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 35, verse 44:

﴿Have they not traveled through the land and observed how was the end of those before them?﴾ This is an argument in support of what precedes it, namely the continuing operation of God's sunnah (sunna, the established way or pattern) in punishing those who deny, through what they witness (p-157) in their journeys to al-Sham, Yemen and Iraq of the traces of the ruin of the former mighty nations. The hamza (interrogative particle) here expresses denial and negation, and the waw (conjunction) is for coordination with an implied clause suited to the context, meaning: did they remain in their dwellings, and "have they not traveled through the land and observed how was the end of those before them?" ﴿And they were greater than them in strength﴾ and longer in lifespans, yet the length of time did not benefit them, and the might of their powers did not avail them. The clause occupies the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal). God's statement ﴿And God is not such that anything in the heavens or on earth could overcome Him﴾, that is, could outrun Him and escape Him, is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraid) confirming what is understood from the preceding about the annihilation of the earlier nations. God's statement ﴿Indeed, He is ever Knowing and Competent﴾, that is, exceedingly so in knowledge and power, and for this reason He knew all of their evil deeds and punished them accordingly, is a causal explanation (ta'lil) for that.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 35, verse 45:**

﴿If Allah were to seize the people﴾ all together ﴿for what they have earned﴾ of misdeeds, as He did with those [before them], ﴿He would not leave upon its back﴾, i.e., upon the back of the earth, ﴿any creature﴾, any living soul moving upon it from the children of Adam. It was also said: [He would not leave] from others as well, [i.e., other creatures], because of the ill effect of their sins. This is related from Ibn Mas'ud and Anas, may Allah be pleased with them both. The first [view] is strengthened by His words, Exalted is He: ﴿but He defers them to a specified term﴾, which is the Day of Resurrection, ﴿so when their term comes, indeed Allah is ever Seeing of His servants﴾. Then He will recompense them at that time for their deeds: if good, then good; and if evil, then evil.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-Malaikah, the eight gates of Paradise will call to him: 'Enter by whichever gate you wish.'"

And Allah knows best.
